analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from canceling workers' health insurance during a lockout.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee, never received a vote or any further action, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company locks out workers to pressure their union before a strike, the lockout often comes with cutting off the workers' employer health insurance. This bill would make that a prohibited unfair labor practice under national labor law, with civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation — doubled to $150,000 for repeat violators in serious cases. It would also allow penalties against company directors or officers who directed or failed to prevent the violation. The bill never got a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers locked out by their employer during a labor dispute, and their families, who would keep their employer health coverage while the lockout lasts. Unions would also gain because maintaining coverage removes one of the company's main economic weapons for pressuring workers at the bargaining table.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds to the National Labor Relations Act a new prohibition: an employer may not terminate or alter an employee's group health plan coverage while locking out, suspending, or withholding employment to influence the employee or their union in collective bargaining before a strike.

Employers that violate the ban face a civil penalty of up to $75,000 per violation, doubled to $150,000 when the violation coincides with a discharge or causes serious economic harm and the employer violated the same rule within the previous five years.

The bill lets the National Labor Relations Board also assess penalties against company directors or officers who directed or committed the violation, or who had knowledge and authority to prevent it and failed to.
The Board must weigh the gravity of the employer's actions, the employer's size, its history of violations, and the public interest when setting the penalty.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use lockouts in labor disputes would bear the cost of keeping health coverage in place during a lockout and of penalties if they cut it anyway. Companies that bargain hard with unions — and, in practice, some workers facing longer lockouts if employers shift tactics — could be affected.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers that lock out unionized workers

drawbacks.text: The bill raises costs for employers in labor disputes: a company would have to keep paying for health coverage of workers it has locked out, which a supporter would acknowledge makes lockouts more expensive to use as a bargaining tool.

The penalty can reach $75,000 per violation and up to $150,000 for repeat violators in cases of serious harm — a real exposure that small employers could find hard to absorb, even though the Board is required to consider employer size when setting the amount.
The protection is narrow: it covers only coverage during a pre-strike lockout and does not address other economic pressures employers may use in bargaining disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted but real: for a locked-out worker, losing family health coverage is one of the harshest blows a lockout delivers, and this bill would remove that weapon while leaving employers free to use other lawful economic pressure. The costs fall on employers that choose to lock out workers, a tactic that is itself relatively rare and aggressive. The main weakness is enforcement: the bill relies on the National Labor Relations Board, whose cases can take years, and the protection applies only to health coverage during pre-strike lockouts.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on May 24, 2022, joined by five Democratic colleagues — Casey, Blumenthal, Whitehouse, Wyden, and Booker.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever recorded: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House counterpart action appear in the bill's history before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use lockouts to pressure unions came out ahead, since they retain the ability to cut locked-out workers' health coverage without facing the bill's penalties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that lock out unionized workers

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar employers from cutting workers' health coverage during a lockout.

for.name: Robert Casey, Richard Blumenthal, Sheldon Whitehouse, Ron Wyden, and Cory Booker

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or action; it sat in the HELP Committee from May 2022 until the Congress ended with no recorded activity.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican supported it, and the Democratic-run committee never advanced the bill to the floor.

industries.industry: Employers that use lockouts in labor disputes
industries.note: These employers currently can cut off health coverage for locked-out workers to increase pressure at the bargaining table; the bill would take that option away and attach penalties of up to $75,000 per violation. Their interest in keeping that leverage runs directly against locked-out workers' access to health care.

industries.industry: Employer group health plans and insurers that administer them
industries.note: The bill would keep premiums and claims flowing during lockouts rather than ending them, preserving coverage revenue, but it does not change how these plans are run or their relationship to workers.
